docs.title: HemOnc Alchemy
docs.text:
HemOnc Alchemy provides Python tools for querying HemOnc.org treatment data. It includes SQLAlchemy models, condition and component searches, regimen selection, dosing schedules, and optional OMOP vocabulary queries.

Use a local DuckDB file or a PostgreSQL database containing the HemOnc tables. Install the driver for your chosen backend and configure the database before running queries. The package includes the model and loader; HemOnc source data and OMOP vocabulary data are supplied separately.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
1. Install with the DuckDB or PostgreSQL extra.
  2. Configure your database.
  3. Follow the quickstart to find treatment variants for a condition.

To create and load a development database, follow Local development.

docs.title: Find the right guide
docs.text:
Task Guide Understand tables, identifiers and relationships The HemOnc model Find conditions, components and linked records Core queries Select or classify treatment variants Treatment analytics Read dosing days or build a treatment timeline Schedules and administration Resolve HemOnc identifiers through OMOP vocabulary OMOP integration

When counting results, check what each row represents. For example, one regimen can have several variants, each with several dosing instructions. A study name can also occur in several condition-specific rows. See Entities and generated models for identifiers and Relationships for study and version-selection rules.

docs.title: Project status
docs.text: HemOnc Alchemy is pre-1.0. APIs and generated schemas may change without a compatibility layer or a migration path.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
You need the Python package and a populated HemOnc database. Choose the backend that suits your environment:

Backend Use it when Install DuckDB You want to query a local database file without a database server. hemonc-alchemy[duckdb] PostgreSQL You have a PostgreSQL database or need shared server access. hemonc-alchemy[postgres]
  1. Install the package with your backend extra.
  2. Configure a database containing the HemOnc tables.
  3. Run the quickstart to find treatment variants for a condition.

If you need to create a database from a source extract, use the local development guide for DuckDB or PostgreSQL, then follow Loading data.

The model guide explains what each row represents and how identifiers and relationships work. Read it before combining tables or counting records.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
HemOnc Alchemy uses oa-configurator so several Australian Cancer Data Network packages can refer to the same named databases without putting credentials in Python or source control.

The configuration has three levels:

  • A connection contains driver, host, credentials, and database name.
  • A database gives that connection a logical name and schema.
  • A tool target selects hemonc_db and an optional CDM target, omop_db, for vocabulary queries.

That indirection is useful when the same application moves between a local database, a shared server, and a test database. It also makes it possible for a HemOnc target and an OMOP target to share a PostgreSQL server while remaining different schemas or databases.

docs.title: Configure a database
docs.text:
Run the interactive configurator:

omop-config configure hemonc_alchemy

A minimal configuration has this shape:

[connections.hemonc]
dialect       = "postgresql+psycopg"
host          = "localhost"
port          = 5432
user          = "hemonc"
password      = "change-me"
database_name = "hemonc_alchemy"

[databases.hemonc_db]
kind        = "generic"
connection  = "hemonc"
schema_name = "public"

[tools.hemonc_alchemy]
hemonc_db = "hemonc_db"

Let the configurator create the real file so its current conventions are preserved. Never commit passwords. If you need separate test or OMOP targets, configure them as additional named databases rather than changing application code.

docs.title: Open a session
docs.text:
Resolve the logical target once, keep the engine for the lifetime of the application, and create sessions for units of work:

from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from hemonc_alchemy import create_hemonc_engine, get_hemonc_context

_, database = get_hemonc_context()
engine = create_hemonc_engine(database)

with Session(engine) as session:
    ...

Toolkit functions do not own your session or transaction. This keeps connection lifetime, transaction boundaries, and error handling under application control.

docs.title: The devcontainer configuration
docs.text:
When the repository devcontainer is created, .devcontainer/config.toml is copied to ~/.config/omop/config.toml with mode 600. Its hemonc_db target points at the Compose PostgreSQL service; its test target points at a separate hemonc_alchemy_test database. HemOnc's generated tables and foreign keys carry the logical primary role. create_hemonc_engine() uses oa-configurator to map that role to the target's configured schema_name, or the connection's default schema when no override is configured.

The checked-in file is a seed, not the active configuration. An existing copy is never overwritten. To keep configuration elsewhere, set OA_CONFIG_PATH before starting Python. OA_CONFIG_SEED chooses the seed used by post-create.sh when that file is absent. Back up a customized config before editing it.

docs.title: DuckDB configuration
docs.text:
Install hemonc-alchemy[duckdb] and use a persistent, writable file. Keep the file stem distinct from the configured schema name: DuckDB uses that stem as its catalog name, and identical names make two-part table references ambiguous.

[connections.local]
dialect = "duckdb"
database_name = "/absolute/writable/path/hemonc-alchemy.duckdb"

[databases.hemonc_db]
kind = "generic"
connection = "local"
schema_name = "hemonc"

[databases.cdm_db]
kind = "cdm"
connection = "local"
cdm_schema = "cdm"
vocab_schema = "omop"

[tools.hemonc_alchemy]
hemonc_db = "hemonc_db"
omop_db = "cdm_db"

Omit the CDM database and omop_db if no vocabulary is needed. Bootstrap creates HemOnc tables; load vocabulary tables separately. A vocabulary join requires the vocabulary role to use the same physical database as HemOnc. Merely sharing a PostgreSQL server is insufficient. A separate schema in the same PostgreSQL database or DuckDB file is supported. See OMOP integration.

The independent DuckDB devcontainer uses .devcontainer/config.duckdb.toml, a separate active config filename, and a database persisted under the repository's data mount. See Local development.

docs.title: Update an existing copied config
docs.text:
Startup preserves an existing file, so dependency upgrades do not apply seed changes to it. Back up the active TOML and apply these changes where applicable:

  1. In [tools.omop_alchemy], rename test_cdm_db to test_cdm_db_pg. Keep its existing database reference; the [databases.test_cdm_db] entry need not be renamed.
  2. In [tools.hemonc_alchemy], add omop_db = "cdm_db" using the intended CDM database's actual name. This makes vocabulary selection explicit when several CDM targets exist.
  3. For copies of the old repository seed, change cdm_schema = "public" to "cdm" in [databases.cdm_db] and [databases.test_cdm_db]. Leave HemOnc's schema_name = "public" and vocab_schema = "omop" intact. oa-configurator 2.1 rejects overlapping explicit primary-schema ownership. These settings route future CDM operations; they do not move existing CDM tables. Adapt this layout to any existing clinical tables before using CDM tooling.

HemOnc-only configs do not need an OMOP target. Existing generic HemOnc targets remain valid. To switch to DuckDB, select a separate config file instead of replacing the PostgreSQL connection in place.

docs.title: Check the connection
docs.text:
python - <<'PY'
from sqlalchemy import text
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from hemonc_alchemy import create_hemonc_engine, get_hemonc_context

_, database = get_hemonc_context()
engine = create_hemonc_engine(database)
with Session(engine) as session:
    print(session.execute(text("SELECT 1")).scalar_one())
PY

If the target is missing, configure it with omop-config configure hemonc_alchemy rather than embedding a connection string in analysis code.

docs.title: Bring your own engine
docs.text:
For a URL-based connection to HemOnc tables in the database's default schema:

from hemonc_alchemy import create_default_hemonc_engine

engine = create_default_hemonc_engine("sqlite:///:memory:")

This helper accepts the usual SQLAlchemy engine keyword arguments and adds schema_translate_map={"primary": None}. Explicit execution options and schema routes take precedence. Existing SQLAlchemy engines can receive that same execution option before creating tables or sessions. For an isolated physical schema, map primary to its name or use the configured target shown above. Mapping does not create the physical schema; provision it before creating the tables.

Raw SQL text is not rewritten by schema translation. SQLAlchemy model and table expressions carry the logical schema role. The role is also part of metadata keys, for example Base.metadata.tables["primary.variants"].

Named PostgreSQL enum types use the same role as their tables. DuckDB uses string columns with label CHECK constraints, avoiding the current driver's untranslated schema references for named enum types while retaining label validation.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: The package contains the SQLAlchemy model, connection helpers and toolkit. Choose an extra for the database you want to query.

docs.title: Use HemOnc from another project
docs.text:
Backend uv pip DuckDB file uv add "hemonc-alchemy[duckdb]" pip install "hemonc-alchemy[duckdb]" PostgreSQL server uv add "hemonc-alchemy[postgres]" pip install "hemonc-alchemy[postgres]"

Then configure the database and run the quickstart.

docs.title: Work on the repository
docs.text:
uv sync --extra dev

Run this command from the repository root. The dev extra adds model-generation tools, tests, linting and documentation dependencies.

docs.title: Run the notebooks
docs.text:
uv sync --extra exploration

The exploration extra adds the Python kernel, matplotlib, IPython, and the PostgreSQL driver used by notebooks/. For package development and notebooks together:

uv sync --extra dev --extra exploration

The repository devcontainers install the development, exploration, PostgreSQL, DuckDB, authoring, and OMOP extras together.

docs.title: Use the OMOP bridge
docs.text:
Add omop when resolving HemOnc identifiers against an OMOP vocabulary. For example, with DuckDB:

uv add "hemonc-alchemy[duckdb,omop]"

When working in this repository, use uv sync --extra dev --extra omop. See OMOP integration for vocabulary configuration and query examples.

docs.title: What installation does not provide
docs.text: Supply a populated HemOnc database or a source extract to import. OMOP queries also need a loaded vocabulary. The local development guide covers creating a DuckDB database or running the PostgreSQL Compose stack.

docs.title: Local development stack
docs.text: Choose the DuckDB path for a local file or the PostgreSQL path for the shared development stack. Neither starts an import automatically. Both install the frozen project environment and seed configuration only when the selected config file does not exist.

docs.title: DuckDB: no PostgreSQL service required
docs.text:
From the repository root:

docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.duckdb.yaml up -d --build

First startup installs the frozen development dependencies before seeding configuration. Wait until the service logs report that the stack config was installed or retained. Follow them with docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.duckdb.yaml logs -f python-hemonc-alchemy-duckdb; press Ctrl-C after setup completes to stop following logs. The service keeps running.

Place licensed source CSVs under data/Tables, then import:

docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.duckdb.yaml exec \
  python-hemonc-alchemy-duckdb uv run python -m hemonc_alchemy.bootstrap

This Compose file runs only a Python service: it needs no PostgreSQL service, shared network, or database port. In VS Code, choose the HemOnc Alchemy — DuckDB development configuration under .devcontainer/duckdb/devcontainer.json. The interpreter is /opt/venv/bin/python.

The seed is .devcontainer/config.duckdb.toml. Its active copy is /home/vscode/.config/omop/hemonc-duckdb.toml; its database is /workspace/hemonc-alchemy/data/hemonc-alchemy.duckdb. The repository mount persists the database on the host at data/hemonc-alchemy.duckdb. Keep this directory writable by the container user. HemOnc uses schema hemonc; optional vocabulary tables use omop, with CDM tables assigned cdm in the same file. Bootstrap imports HemOnc only; it does not supply an OMOP vocabulary.

Use one process to write a DuckDB file. Stop other processes using the file before a bootstrap or rebuild; multiple writer processes are unsupported. Multiple processes can read with database.create_engine(register_claims=False, connect_args={"read_only": True}) when no writer is running. Sessions within one process can share an engine. Do not commit the database or licensed extracts.

Stop this independent stack with:

docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.duckdb.yaml down

docs.title: PostgreSQL: existing shared development stack
docs.text:
The default .devcontainer/devcontainer.json starts PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector, the Python service, and pgAdmin. Create the network shared with SCOOP before starting:

docker network inspect hemonc-alchemy_default >/dev/null 2>&1 || \
  docker network create hemonc-alchemy_default
docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml up -d --build

Wait for initial Python service setup and config seeding to finish. Open the repository in VS Code's default Dev Container, or import from the Python service:

docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml exec \
  python-hemonc-alchemy uv run python -m hemonc_alchemy.bootstrap

The seed .devcontainer/config.toml targets the Compose postgres service. HemOnc uses public, CDM uses cdm, and vocabulary uses omop. A separate test database keeps PostgreSQL tests away from the loaded development database. See Configuration before using an older copied seed.

pgAdmin is available at http://localhost:5050. Set login values in .devcontainer/.env before using a shared machine. Connect to host postgres, port 5432, database hemonc_alchemy, user hemonc. Inside pgAdmin, localhost refers to its own container.

docs.title: Import and rebuild behavior
docs.text:
Bootstrap selects the active oa-configurator hemonc_db target. It creates all generated HemOnc tables and imports the source files it finds. --data-dir selects another extract directory; repeat --table to select specific source tables. Missing or ambiguous selected files fail before database changes.

An existing HemOnc table makes the default import fail. For a disposable target, add --rebuild to reset all HemOnc tables and recognized HemOnc staging objects in the selected schema. Unrelated and vocabulary tables are retained. This is not an incremental reload. A failed import may leave committed parent rows; fix the source and explicitly rebuild the disposable target. See Loading data.

Existing active config files are retained on restart and rebuild. Set OA_CONFIG_PATH before launching Python to choose a different file; OA_CONFIG_SEED selects a create-time seed. Switching seeds does not overwrite an existing file.

docs.title: Notebooks and tests
docs.text:
Both development paths install the development, authoring, exploration, PostgreSQL, DuckDB, and OMOP extras. Open notebooks with /opt/venv/bin/python. _setup.open_session() reports whether it connected to the configured database or used the small demo dataset.

Run these commands inside the chosen Python service:

uv run pytest
uv run pytest -m duckdb -o addopts=''

Run PostgreSQL tests in the PostgreSQL path with uv run pytest -m postgres -o addopts=''. The default pytest selection excludes database-dialect tests, so run the selected backend suite explicitly.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Find treatment variants by looking up a condition's HemOnc CUI and passing it to a selection query.

This example works with a configured DuckDB or PostgreSQL database containing the HemOnc tables. See Configuration to set up the connection.

from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from hemonc_alchemy import create_hemonc_engine, get_hemonc_context
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.core.conditions import condition_cuis_by_names
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.analytics.treatment.selection import (
    TreatmentSelectionSpec,
    select_variants,
)

_, database = get_hemonc_context()
engine = create_hemonc_engine(database)

with Session(engine) as session:
    condition_cuis = condition_cuis_by_names(session, "Acute myeloid leukemia")
    if not condition_cuis:
        raise LookupError("Condition was not found")

    spec = TreatmentSelectionSpec.for_conditions(
        condition_cuis,
        version_policy="latest",
    )
    variants = select_variants(session, spec)

    for variant in variants[:5]:
        print(variant.variant_cui, variant.version, variant.regimen)

version_policy="latest" selects the highest imported (version, id) per variant_cui before applying condition filters. Use version_policy="all" to query imported versions together. See Variant versions and sigs for how this differs from the source-defined current version.

docs.title: Inspect a selected variant
docs.text:
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.analytics.treatment.bundles import VariantBundle

with Session(engine) as session:
    variants = select_variants(session, spec)
    if variants:
        bundle = VariantBundle.from_variant(variants[0])
        for sig in bundle.sigs:
            print(sig.component, sig.doseminnum, sig.doseunit, sig.alldays)

Keep the session open while reading related records. Sigs link through variant_cui without a version, so these instructions are shared across imported versions with that CUI.

docs.title: Inspect or extend the SQL
docs.text:
Use a statement builder to add filters or limits before running a query:

from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.core.components import component_search_statement

statement = component_search_statement("cisplatin").limit(20)
with Session(engine) as session:
    rows = session.execute(statement).mappings().all()

For treatment selection, build_variant_query_artifacts() exposes the intermediate projections as well as the final statement. This is useful when a selection returns an unexpected number of variants.

docs.title: Updating an existing setup
docs.text: HemOnc Alchemy is currently a beta release only. APIs and generated schemas may change without a compatibility layer or a migration path. When updating, check the package, configuration, database schema and application calls together.

docs.title: Install the backend you use
docs.text:
In an application managed with uv, update the package with your backend extra:

uv add --upgrade "hemonc-alchemy[duckdb]"

For PostgreSQL, use hemonc-alchemy[postgres]. Add omop to the extras if your application uses the vocabulary integration, for example hemonc-alchemy[duckdb,omop]. See Installation for repository development environments.

docs.title: Check your configuration
docs.text:
The application uses the named hemonc_db target. An optional omop_db selects the vocabulary target. Configuration files are retained across environment rebuilds, so compare an existing file with the current configuration examples. The copied-config checklist covers older repository seeds.

Use create_hemonc_engine() for a configured target or create_default_hemonc_engine() for tables in a URL connection's default schema. Both map the model's logical primary schema role. See Engine configuration for custom SQLAlchemy engines.

docs.title: Use a database built for the model
docs.text:
An existing database must have the columns and tables expected by the installed model. If the schema differs, import the source into a fresh target. Running table creation against an existing database does not update its tables.

Follow Loading data for imports and rejection reports. For a disposable development target, the bootstrap command can rebuild and reload HemOnc tables. Rebuilding deletes the target's HemOnc data; select the target carefully.

Generated row IDs belong to their imported dataset. Record links using those IDs must refer to the database they came from.

docs.title: Check application queries
docs.text:
Use the model guide to check entity fields and the toolkit guides for current query examples. Verify the pages or analyses that depend on those queries against the rebuilt database.

If the application uses OMOP, check vocabulary availability and routing separately. Some helpers require HemOnc and vocabulary tables in the same physical database; others accept separate sessions. See OMOP integration.

docs.title: OMOP integration
docs.text: The OMOP bridge provides optional read-only queries between HemOnc source records and an OMOP vocabulary. Individual query helpers specify whether they use one database session or accept separate source and vocabulary sessions.

docs.title: The mental model
docs.text:
There are three identifiers in a typical mapping:

Identifier Meaning HemOnc CUI The source identity used by HemOnc tables, such as condition_cui=614 HemOnc OMOP concept_id The surrogate ID for the corresponding row in the registered HemOnc vocabulary Target OMOP concept_id The concept in a target vocabulary such as SNOMED or RxNorm

The bridge keeps all three distinct. A CUI is used as concept_code in the HemOnc OMOP vocabulary, but it is not an OMOP concept_id.

Mapping is one-to-many. map_to_standard() returns one object per active Maps to edge, with the relationship label and both concept references intact. It does not select the first target and it does not reinterpret treatment relationships such as Has cytotox chemo Rx as ordinary vocabulary mappings.

docs.title: Installation and configuration
docs.text:
Install the optional dependency when you need the integration package:

uv add "hemonc-alchemy[omop]"

The bridge lazily loads OMOP Alchemy's public CDM models and uses their validity semantics. The HemOnc package does not import the optional model tree during ordinary package imports. HemOnc-specific mapping joins remain local because OMOP Alchemy cannot know which HemOnc CUI or relationship policy a consumer intends.

Set [tools.hemonc_alchemy].omop_db to the intended CDM database entry in oa-configurator. The bridge adds that target's vocab route to the HemOnc bind while preserving HemOnc's primary route. The repository seeds use separate schemas: public (PostgreSQL) or hemonc (DuckDB) for source tables, and omop for vocabulary. Sharing a default schema is also supported when configured. Both roles must reach the same physical database for SQL joins. See Configuration for the TOML layout and existing-config upgrade steps.

Use availability diagnostics before optional queries:

from hemonc_alchemy.integrations.omop import omop_availability, map_to_standard

status = omop_availability(session, require_relationships=True)
if status.available:
    mappings = map_to_standard(session, [105], target_vocabulary="RxNorm")
else:
    print(status.reason)

With no omop extra installed, availability is false and optional query helpers remain no-ops. With the extra installed but unreachable vocabulary tables, availability reports the schema route and database failure; guarded query helpers raise OmopUnavailableError. An unavailable vocabulary is therefore distinguishable from a valid query with no mapping rows. Ordinary HemOnc imports do not require a vocabulary or load the OMOP model tree.

For an explicit application-owned context, resolve a ResolvedCDMDatabase and route the session before calling query helpers:

from oa_configurator import Resolver
from hemonc_alchemy.integrations.omop import schema_aware_bind

vocabulary = Resolver.from_active_config().resolve_database("cdm_db")
schema_aware_bind(session, omop_database=vocabulary)

omop_availability(session, omop_database=vocabulary) accepts the same context. Explicit schema_translate_map={"vocab": "omop"} overrides configuration and retains existing routes; this remains useful for manually attached test schemas. Explicit context selection takes precedence over automatic discovery. An existing vocabulary map is retained unless explicitly replaced. For an unselected generic HemOnc target, legacy discovery accepts exactly one matching CDM vocabulary target; multiple matches report ambiguity and require omop_db. A bind already identified as a CDM target uses its own vocabulary role.

docs.title: Common queries
docs.text:
from hemonc_alchemy.integrations.omop import (
    condition_to_snomed,
    drug_to_rxnorm_ingredient,
    regimen_to_hemonc,
)

condition_rows = condition_to_snomed(session, [614])
drug_rows = drug_to_rxnorm_ingredient(session, [105])
regimen_rows = regimen_to_hemonc(session, [2204])

For the loaded development database, the first two examples resolve as follows:

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (CUI 614)
  → HemOnc concept_id 42542184
  → SNOMED code 118599009

Cisplatin (CUI 105)
  → HemOnc concept_id 35802958
  → RxNorm code 2555

docs.title: Diagnostics are part of the result
docs.text:
Use coverage_report() when a mapping is used as an analytical denominator. It reports requested, resolved, mapped, unmatched, and ambiguous CUIs and includes the advertised versions from omop.vocabulary. A missing mapping means “not present in this vocabulary release” unless the source and target data have been independently audited; it does not prove that the concept does not exist.

The biomarker_qualifier_diagnostics() helper is advisory. Molecularly qualified HemOnc conditions can map to an unqualified SNOMED disorder or fail to map. Keep the HemOnc condition CUI and qualifier fields when this distinction matters. suspicious_condition_mappings() surfaces condition edges to modifier/measurement concepts for vocabulary review; it does not automatically delete or rewrite them.

docs.title: Relationship taxonomy
docs.text:
OMOP contains useful HemOnc-native relationships in this deployment:

  • regimen_modalities() reads Has modality links.
  • component_roles() reads the directed component-role relationships and keeps their labels separate.
  • component_class_hierarchy() reads direct Is a links to Component Class nodes.
  • main_class_ancestry() combines source drug groups with the hierarchy to classify endocrine and growth-factor ancestry. See Classify drug ancestry for querying, applying and inspecting the results.

These are curated HemOnc taxonomy edges, not a replacement for public.indications. Regulatory indication data in the HemOnc table is richer and has different semantics and coverage.

docs.title: Database boundary
docs.text:
The mapping and relationship query helpers perform same-database joins. Resolved vocabulary targets in another physical database are rejected before connecting to that target; there is no automatic attach or cross-database join. Only the vocabulary role must be local: the selected CDM target can keep its clinical primary in another database while sharing a local vocabulary connection.

If HemOnc and OMOP vocabulary are in separate databases, query the source CUIs first and resolve them with a second OMOP session. main_class_ancestry(source_session, omop_session=vocabulary_session) handles this separation directly, combining the query results in Python. PostgreSQL being on the same server is not enough for an ordinary cross-database SQL join. Other queries require an explicit application-level bridge, an FDW, or a materialized mapping subset.

docs.title: Regenerating the model
docs.text: The generated model is a build artifact of the HemOnc data dictionary. Regeneration is therefore a schema change to review, not an ordinary edit to Python files.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
Install the development tools, then run:

uv sync --extra dev
hemonc-alchemy validate
hemonc-alchemy diff
hemonc-alchemy regen --data-dir path/to/extract

Review the generated diff before accepting it. If a source table has intentionally disappeared, use the command's explicit acceptance flag rather than allowing source loss to pass silently.

Run the checks before committing:

pytest
ruff check hemonc_alchemy tests
lint-imports

docs.title: Generated versus hand-written code
docs.text: Do not hand-edit model/entities.py, model/enums.py, or schema/registry.json. Change the source data dictionary or compiler behavior, regenerate, and review the output. Hand-written relationships belong in model/relationships.py; reusable query and interpretation code belongs in the toolkit.

docs.title: Release and repository workflow
docs.text: HemOnc Alchemy uses the shared cava-devops workflows. The package repository keeps the small amount of configuration that is inherently repository-specific; the CI, label gate, release drafting, documentation deployment, and distribution build logic remains reusable and centralised.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
The CI workflow runs on pull requests targeting main:

  • label-gate / check requires exactly one release label: breaking, feature, fix, dependencies, or chore.
  • default / test runs the default dialect-independent suite without a database service.
  • duckdb / test explicitly selects duckdb tests through CAVA's shared DuckDB workflow.
  • postgres / test runs the shared PostgreSQL service workflow with PYTEST_ADDOPTS=-m postgres. The required-connection flag makes unavailable PostgreSQL fixtures fail instead of silently skipping the dialect job.
  • installed-wheel / wheel (core) and installed-wheel / wheel (duckdb-omop) install built wheels in clean environments and exercise them outside the checkout.

build-test / test retains the organization-required check name and passes only when all four validation jobs succeed. It runs even after a failed, cancelled or skipped dependency, so a skipped job cannot bypass the merge gate.

The project default excludes both db_dialect and legacy postgres markers. The PostgreSQL override and DuckDB workflow command explicitly replace that selection. Licensed full-extract parity is a separate local release gate; public CI uses synthetic fixtures and skips real-extract checks when their inputs are absent. See the repository's validation instructions.

The label controls release intent, not test selection. Use chore for documentation, refactoring, generated maintenance, and CI changes that should not create a release-note entry. Use the highest applicable bump label when a change affects the public package.

The PR title becomes the release-note entry. The description is reviewer context, so explain design decisions, data-model consequences, and how the change was verified there. Before merging, confirm that the title is suitable for someone reading the release history months later.

docs.title: Versioning and release drafting
docs.text:
The version is derived from Git tags by hatch-vcs. The repository does not maintain a manually edited version string or a generated CHANGELOG.md.

When a labelled PR is squash-merged, merge.yml updates the standing draft release. The draft's next version is resolved from the highest-priority label it contains:

Label Version impact breaking Major feature Minor fix or dependencies Patch chore No release-note entry and no version bump

A maintainer reviews and publishes the draft from GitHub's Releases page. Publishing creates a vX.Y.Z tag on main; that tag is the only event that starts package publication.

The shared workflow's label-to-version rules also apply while this package is pre-1.0. In particular, breaking selects a major bump; review the proposed version before publishing. API and schema compatibility are not pre-1.0 release requirements.

docs.title: Package publication
docs.text:
publish.yml delegates building to CAVA, which verifies that the tag is reachable from main and produces the wheel and source distribution. The final PyPI upload stays in this repository because PyPI trusted publishing binds its OIDC identity to the calling repository's workflow file.

The repository needs a GitHub environment named pypi and a PyPI trusted publisher with these values:

Field Value Owner AustralianCancerDataNetwork Repository hemonc-alchemy Workflow publish.yml Environment pypi

docs.title: Documentation deployment
docs.text: docs.yml deploys the MkDocs site after changes land on main and can also be run manually. The documentation dependencies live in the dev extra so the reusable deployment workflow can recreate the same build environment.

docs.title: Repository settings
docs.text:
The existing organization rules require pull requests, at least one approval, and these status checks on main:

  • label-gate / check
  • build-test / test

The aggregate build-test / test requires the default, DuckDB, PostgreSQL, and installed-wheel jobs. This protects every validation axis without changing a shared organization ruleset to include repository-specific check names.

Use squash merging as the normal merge strategy and prevent force pushes to main. The initial history migration or other exceptional administrative operation should be handled separately from ordinary package changes.

docs.title: Understanding the HemOnc model
docs.text: The generated SQLAlchemy model is a typed view of the imported source. It tells you what rows and fields exist; it does not decide what a row means for a particular application. That distinction is why the toolkit sits above the model.

docs.title: The core row grains
docs.text:
Entity One row represents Conditions A HemOnc condition and its CUI Regimens A named regimen Variants A concrete regimen variant and imported version Sigs One dosing instruction within a variant Drugs A treatment component or drug identity Studies A study/source row associated with HemOnc content StudyResults A recorded outcome from a study Indications A regulatory indication and its evidence metadata

These grains are deliberately different. Counting sigs answers a question about dosing instructions, not regimens. Counting indications answers a question about regulatory records, not distinct drugs. A join can multiply rows even when every table is correct.

docs.title: Read the model in layers
docs.text:
flowchart TD Tables[Generated entity tables] --> Maps[Generated child map tables] Tables --> Relations[Read-only cross-reference relationships] Relations --> Toolkit[Core and treatment toolkit]
  • Generated entities describe table shape.
  • Generated child maps preserve multi-valued source fields in normalized form.
  • Hand-written relationships provide convenient traversal but do not change source identity.
  • Toolkit functions add reusable query or treatment policy.

Start with the generated class when you need a structural query. Move to the toolkit when the operation involves recurring cross-reference logic, version policy, treatment classification, or schedule interpretation.

docs.title: The identity model
docs.text:
There are three identities to keep distinct:

  1. A generated database row has a surrogate id.
  2. A HemOnc concept has a source CUI such as condition_cui or drug_cui.
  3. An OMOP concept has an OMOP concept_id.

The same value should not be used interchangeably across those roles. See Entities and generated models and Relationships and cross-references before writing joins.

docs.title: Entities and generated models
docs.text: The classes in hemonc_alchemy.model are generated from the HemOnc data dictionary. Treat them as a faithful structural surface: application-specific state, protocol rules, and derived classifications belong outside the generated model.

docs.title: Choosing a class
docs.text:
Use the entity that matches the question's grain:

  • Conditions for condition identity and names.
  • Regimens for named treatment concepts and regimen-level metadata.
  • Variants for concrete regimen versions.
  • Sigs for drug, dose, route, and cycle-day instructions.
  • Drugs for component identity and classification.
  • Indications for regulatory records.
  • Studies and StudyResults for source studies and recorded outcomes.

For example:

from hemonc_alchemy import Sigs, Variants

variant = session.get(Variants, variant_id)
if variant is not None:
    for sig in variant.component_sigs:
        print(sig.component, sig.alldays)

docs.title: Surrogate IDs and source keys
docs.text:
Generated primary keys make relationships efficient, but they are not usually the source identity. For Variants:

database primary key: id
source/version key:   (variant_cui, version)
latest identity:      variant_cui, when a latest-version policy is explicit

Child map rows use generated foreign keys. For example, variants_study.parent_id points to Variants.id, not Variants.variant_cui.

docs.title: Generated enums
docs.text:
Enum columns are exposed as generated Python enum members:

from hemonc_alchemy.model.enums import Sigs_RouteEnum

if sig.route == Sigs_RouteEnum.INTRAVENOUS:
    ...

Toolkit functions that accept source-facing strings document their normalization rules. In lower-level SQLAlchemy expressions, prefer the generated enum member for enum columns.

docs.title: HemOnc CUIs and OMOP concepts
docs.text: A HemOnc CUI is a source identifier, not an OMOP concept_id. When the HemOnc vocabulary is loaded into OMOP, the CUI can be found as concept_code with vocabulary_id = 'HemOnc'; an external mapping then leads to a target vocabulary and target code. These are separate joins with separate semantics.

docs.title: Loading data
docs.text: Loading is an environment or maintainer operation. Analysis code should normally connect to an already imported database and use the model or toolkit.

docs.title: Load one entity
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

from hemonc_alchemy.model import Variants
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.loading import load_all

counts = load_all(session, Variants, Path("data/Tables"))
session.commit()
print(counts)

load_all() loads primary rows and their denormalized child tables. It resolves source filenames and headers, applies an explicit HemOnc conversion policy, and maps child rows back to accepted parents. Its return value remains a dictionary of counts; load_entity() returns the primary count and load_denormalised() returns child counts.

docs.title: Loader 3 compatibility
docs.text:
HemOnc uses orm-loader 3, oa-configurator 2.1, and optional omop-alchemy 3. Install the DuckDB driver with uv sync --extra duckdb; PostgreSQL remains available with --extra postgres. Both backends support the configured devcontainer workflow. Use a configured engine or create_default_hemonc_engine() so the generated primary schema role is mapped before creating tables or loading rows.

Entity classes now provide load_file(session, path, ...). load_csv() remains a deprecated compatibility alias. register_enum_casts() remains callable but is unnecessary: conversion is local to each load and does not modify an upstream global cast registry.

An ID-less CSV for a surrogate-key entity requires an empty parent table. PostgreSQL and DuckDB reserve IDs from the table's native sequence; subsequent ORM inserts continue from that sequence. SQLite uses the public loader ID allocator for these BIGINT columns. This snapshot path assumes a single writer. A second ID-less import raises before staging; use a fresh disposable target or a source with stable, explicit IDs. Incremental identity reconciliation is not implemented.

PostgreSQL reserves sequence values on an additional connection because later file batches are read while COPY is active on the loader connection. Its pool must allow that additional connection. Create and commit the schema before beginning the snapshot import.

Files supplying IDs use the upstream merge strategies. Callers supplying explicit IDs are responsible for synchronizing native sequences before later inserts that omit IDs. Child loading uses plain inserts and is not an idempotent reload operation.

For ID-less snapshots, the loader retains each parsed source occurrence's assigned ID until its child load completes. Rejected parent IDs are excluded. Thus two sig rows with the same scalar values can keep different study lists, and two exact duplicate occurrences can each retain their children. This association uses the assigned IDs, not the order returned by a database query.

When calling load_entity() and load_denormalised() separately, use the same Session, unchanged source file, and matching CSV reading options. A commit between stages is supported; a rollback discards the retained association. Supplied IDs and unambiguous scalar identities support independent child loads, but ambiguous fallback matches raise an error rather than silently omit children. A changed file or reading options also raises before child insertion. Custom readers must preserve the source record order and parsing rules used by child loading; splitting batches is supported.

Only | is automatically inferred and split as a collection delimiter. Semicolons remain part of names or prose: for example, GEICAM/2003-11; CIBOMA/2004-01 is one study name with CUI 25246. Dictionary overrides define reference names, study names, sig notes, and parenthetical expressions as scalar fields.

docs.title: Source fields and types
docs.text:
The generated model determines how each field is stored. For example, StudyResults.metric_num_this_arm stores values such as 60% as text, Persons.total_pubs is an integer, and the four Refs.prop_valid_aff_* fields are numeric proportions. Fields listed in the model metadata's derived_columns are excluded from source loading.

Text fields retain their values apart from configured null markers, while dates and enums undergo conversion. Unsupported partial dates in nullable DateTime fields become NULL, and enum conversion normalizes source spelling. A database NULL can therefore represent either a missing source value or a failed conversion; use the source file and rejection report to distinguish them.

docs.title: Conversion and rejection reports
docs.text:
The default HemOnc policy preserves case-insensitive enum values and the compiler's normalized-member fallback. Malformed nullable fields are logged and become NULL. Malformed required values reject their rows rather than introducing a sentinel. Rejected parents cannot contribute child rows, including when an accepted parent has the same natural key.

The policy treats NULL, None, N/A, NaN, nan, null, NA, and n/a as text null markers. Dates use the upstream declared formats (yyyymmdd, dd-mon-yyyy, and yyyy-mm-dd); unrecognized nullable date values become NULL. Source markers stored in string columns remain strings unless they are one of the configured null markers. Ambiguous date formats require an explicit handler.

from orm_loader.loaders import LoadReport

report = LoadReport()
counts = load_all(session, Variants, Path("data/Tables"), report=report, resolved=database)
print(report.rows_read, report.rows_rejected, report.accounted)
print(report.rejects_path)

Here database is the resolved target from get_hemonc_context(). Pass it through as resolved=; DuckDB requires it to classify foreign-key enforcement. The report describes the primary file, while the returned dictionary includes child counts. load_entity() keeps rejection CSVs under data_dir/rejects even when it normalizes a source through a temporary file. Treat these reports as source data when storing or sharing them.

To raise on malformed values, including nullable ones, pass an explicit policy. load_all() passes it to both primary and child conversion:

from dataclasses import replace
from orm_loader.conversion import ErrorPolicy
from hemonc_alchemy.model.ingestion import conversion_policy

strict = replace(conversion_policy(), errors=ErrorPolicy(on_error="raise"))
counts = load_all(session, Variants, Path("data/Tables"), policy=strict, resolved=database)

docs.title: Transaction boundaries
docs.text: The upstream file loader commits primary merges internally and can commit intermediate batches. A later child-load failure does not roll back those committed parents; session.rollback() only rolls back work still in the current transaction. Use a disposable target for snapshot imports and rebuild it after a partial failure. Complete schema rebuilding is a separate bootstrap operation.

docs.title: Bootstrap the development database
docs.text:
uv run python -m hemonc_alchemy.bootstrap --data-dir data/Tables

Bootstrap resolves the active hemonc_db with get_hemonc_context(), uses create_hemonc_engine(), and passes the resolved target and primary staging role through to load_all(). It ignores the legacy DATABASE_URL variable. .devcontainer/bootstrap.py remains a thin wrapper for the same entry point.

The default operation creates all generated tables and loads the source files present. It refuses a target already containing any HemOnc table. Repeat --table, for example --table units --table hemonc_classes, to select source tables explicitly. Unknown, missing selected, ambiguous, or entirely absent source files fail before opening the engine or rebuilding anything.

For an existing disposable target, explicitly pass --rebuild. This drops generated HemOnc tables and recognized _staging_<hemonc_table> objects only in the configured HemOnc schema, then recreates the metadata before importing. It retains unrelated tables, unrelated staging objects, and OMOP vocabulary tables. It does not drop the schema or use cascading drops. External foreign keys referencing HemOnc can therefore block a rebuild. Selecting --table limits imported files, not the set of tables reset by --rebuild.

Rebuilds destroy the selected target's HemOnc data. Use only a disposable development target and stop other DuckDB processes using the file first. Each entity can commit before later entities or children fail; retry a partial snapshot with an explicit rebuild after fixing the failure. Programmatic callers can use bootstrap_database(resolved, data_dir, rebuild=False, table_names=None) from hemonc_alchemy.bootstrap and receive per-entity count dictionaries.

docs.title: Relationships and cross-references
docs.text: Child tables use foreign keys to link each value to its parent row. Cross-references between source entities use names or CUIs; these are exposed as read-only ORM relationships and can resolve to several rows.

docs.title: Multi-valued source fields
docs.text:
The loader splits pipe-delimited collections into child rows. For a variant's study references, each row in variants_study contains one study token and the parent variant's ID:

flowchart TB V["variantsid"] -->|"study_items: one to many"| M["variants_studyparent_idstudy"]

variants_study.parent_id references variants.id. Use variant.study_items to read the stored tokens. Each item's study_objects resolves its token to matching Studies rows, including study--substudy references. The same parent/child structure is used for collections on sigs, indications and other entities.

variant.study_objects is a separate, generated relationship that matches bare study names only. Use the map item's study_objects when references include a substudy.

docs.title: Traversal helpers
docs.text:
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.core.links import (
    condition_variant_objects,
    sig_condition_objects,
    sig_study_objects,
    study_variant_objects,
)

conditions = sig_condition_objects(sig)
studies = sig_study_objects(sig)
variants = study_variant_objects(study)

Keep entities attached to their SQLAlchemy session while using these helpers: resolving related rows can issue additional queries.

docs.title: Study references and counts
docs.text:
Studies.study is not unique. A study associated with several conditions can have a row for each condition, so a name lookup can return several rows. Use .scalars().all() unless your query also constrains the row sufficiently to establish uniqueness.

The study catalogue, sig search, component selection and standalone-radiation queries accept bare study names and study--substudy references. So do Studies.variants and each variant study-map item's study_objects. Other generated name-based relationships compare the stored name literally.

The regimen catalogue's study_count counts distinct Studies.id values. For example, two condition-specific rows for one study CUI contribute two to that count.

docs.title: Study-context filters
docs.text:
For a study_context filter, a StudyResults row must match the selected Studies row on study CUI, substudy CUI, condition CUI and biomarker finding. If the result has no study CUI, its exact study name is used instead. A different, non-NULL CUI cannot match by name. For the substudy, condition and biomarker fields, two NULL values count as equal.

A context field containing consolidation|maintenance matches either complete token. Searching for maintenance does not match maintenance extended; % and _ are treated as literal characters. A filter containing | matches only the complete stored field.

docs.title: Variant versions and sigs
docs.text:
One variant_cui can have several imported versions. The following accessors select them differently:

Accessor Selection rule sig.variant_object The source-defined current version, version == 1; None if absent. study_variant_objects(study) Highest (version, id) per CUI among variants linked to that study. Catalogue version_policy="latest" Highest (version, id) per CUI across all imported variants, selected before study and condition filters.

The highest numeric version is not the same rule as the source-defined current version. A study-linked historical version can be returned by study_variant_objects() even when the catalogue's latest selection excludes it.

Sigs store variant_cui without a version. The same sigs are therefore associated with every imported variant version sharing that CUI; those links cannot establish which instructions belonged to a particular historical version.

docs.title: Toolkit
docs.text: The toolkit provides searches, treatment selection and schedule calculations over the imported HemOnc tables. Query functions accept a SQLAlchemy session; scheduling functions work with the selected variants and their sigs.

docs.title: Choose an operation
docs.text: Task Functions and examples Resolve condition names or search components Core queries Follow links between sigs, studies, conditions and variants Traversal helpers Select variants by condition, component or category Treatment selection Classify radiation, systemic or drug-ancestry groups Treatment classification Read dosing days, build administration frames or calculate timelines Scheduling

docs.title: Run a query or build a statement
docs.text:
Execution helpers run a query using your session and return results:

from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.core.components import search_components

hits = search_components(session, "cisplatin")

Statement builders return a SQLAlchemy statement that you can extend before execution:

from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.core.components import component_search_statement

statement = component_search_statement("cisplatin").limit(20)
rows = session.execute(statement).mappings().all()

Return types vary by operation: searches can return result records, selection helpers return ORM entities, and schedule projections return pandas DataFrames. Each guide shows how to read its results.

Keep ORM entities attached to their session while accessing related rows. See Configuration for creating an engine and session.

docs.title: Core queries and links
docs.text: Use toolkit.core to resolve condition names, search treatment components, select sigs by condition, and follow links between records.

docs.title: Resolve names to CUIs
docs.text:
Look up a condition by name and use its HemOnc CUI in subsequent queries:

from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.core.conditions import (
    condition_cuis_by_names,
    conditions_by_names,
)

conditions = conditions_by_names(session, "Acute myeloid leukemia")
condition_cuis = condition_cuis_by_names(session, "Acute myeloid leukemia")

Matching is exact. Missing names are omitted and logged rather than raised. If an absent condition would make the analysis invalid, check the returned list immediately and fail with an application-level message.

The returned CUI is a HemOnc identifier, not an OMOP concept_id. When an OMOP-shaped vocabulary contains HemOnc, the CUI can be looked up as concept_code with vocabulary_id = 'HemOnc'. That is different from following an external mapping to a target vocabulary.

docs.title: Search components
docs.text:
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.core.components import search_components

hits = search_components(session, "cisplatin")
for hit in hits:
    print(hit.component_cui, hit.component, hit.drug_inn, hit.main_class)

The default search is case-insensitive substring matching over the sig component label, drug name and INN, main class, and normalized CanMED major/minor class rows. Pass explicit columns when the vocabulary scope matters; a class-label search and a drug-name search answer different questions.

Use component_search_statement() when you need SQLAlchemy composition, and component_cui_subquery() when the component match is only one predicate in a larger query. CanMED child rows join through generated Drugs.id, not through a drug CUI.

docs.title: Follow model links
docs.text:
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.core.links import (
    condition_variant_objects,
    sig_condition_objects,
    sig_study_objects,
    study_variant_objects,
)

conditions = sig_condition_objects(sig)
studies = sig_study_objects(sig)
variants = study_variant_objects(study)

Keep entities attached to their session while following links. A study name can resolve to several rows, and variant helpers apply the version-selection rules described in the model guide.

docs.title: Select condition-scoped sigs
docs.text:
Use SigSelectionSpec for candidates that are not naturally retrieved through a regimen-variant selection, such as standalone radiotherapy or surgery:

from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.core import SigSelectionSpec, find_sigs

spec = SigSelectionSpec.for_conditions(
    [condition_cui],
    component_terms="External beam radiotherapy",
    variant_policy="none",
)
sigs = find_sigs(session, spec)

The condition restriction is resolved through normalized sigs_study links. The spec can also constrain regimen, phase, class field, study context, and the columns used for component matching. sig_search_statement(spec) returns the inspectable statement without executing it.

Sigs do not carry a version column. A sig selection therefore says which sig rows match; it does not establish version-specific provenance for a variant.

docs.title: Source withdrawal markers
docs.text:
The indication resolver sets ResolvedIndication.withdrawn from the source marker:

Source marker withdrawn Blank or FALSE False TRUE, a date, or any other nonempty marker True

Case and surrounding whitespace are ignored when setting the flag. The original marker is available unchanged in raw["withdrawn"].

Date markers occur on both withdrawal notices and marked authorisation rows. The flag excludes marked records conservatively; a false flag alone does not establish that an authorisation is active. The marker is not parsed into an event type or date.

Regulatory catalogue associations include historical records, without filtering on this flag. Use the resolver flag when excluding marked indication records from your own results.

docs.title: Schedules and administration
docs.text:
Use these helpers to read dosing instructions or calculate a treatment timeline from a variant's sigs. Keep the variant attached to its session while related sigs and drugs are loaded.

Output Function Use it for Parsed cycle days resolve_all_days() Reading one alldays expression. One instruction per sig schedule_events() Inspecting source dose, route, phase and cycle fields. Drug/day DataFrame administration_frame() Comparing administration patterns by drug and route. Sig-level timeline DataFrame roll_out_variant() Following phases and repeated cycles, with dates where timing can be calculated.

docs.title: Read cycle days
docs.text:
from hemonc_alchemy import resolve_all_days

resolved = resolve_all_days("1,8,15,(+n)")
[day.value for day in resolved.days]  # [1, 8, 15]
resolved.indefinite.kind             # "+n"

The continuation marker means the written days are only part of the course. Optional days carry Day.optional=True. Unreadable tokens are logged and dropped; an empty day list can indicate an unresolved schedule.

A pipe means a choice of days, with no selected alternative:

resolved = resolve_all_days("7|8|9|10|11|12|13|14|15")
resolved.days                # ()
resolved.choices[0].options   # [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]

A numeric continuation such as (+2) records an interval of two days in alldays, or two cycles in timing_sequence. Continuation markers retain the interval without generating future events.

docs.title: Inspect dosing instructions
docs.text:
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.analytics.treatment.scheduling import schedule_events

for event in schedule_events(variant):
    print(event.sig.id, event.dose_min, event.dose_max, event.dose_unit)
    print(event.cycle_length_lb, event.cycle_length_ub, event.cycle_length_unit)

ScheduleEvent retains dose and cycle-length bounds in their source form. For example, a bound containing "1.5-2" is text and needs an explicit interpretation before numeric analysis. Generated enum fields are enum members. raw_all_days contains the original dosing-day expression.

docs.title: Build an administration frame
docs.text:
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.analytics.treatment.scheduling import (
    administration_frame,
    administration_matrix,
)

frame = administration_frame(variant, decay_days=0)
clinic = frame[frame.route_group == "IV"]
matrix = administration_matrix(frame, route="IV")

The frame combines instructions for the same variant, drug, route and day. Repeated cycles have separate rows where elapsed_day can be calculated. Pass a list of variants for a combined frame and group results by variant_cui.

Column Meaning day Day within a cycle; lead-in days can be negative. It repeats across cycles. elapsed_day Day relative to variant start; NULL when that position cannot be calculated. route_group IV groups clinic-administered routes, including some non-intravenous routes; PO groups home-administered routes. intensity Projection weight for the day, including optional-day weighting and any decay tail. optional Whether the dosing day or cycle is optional. indefinite, cycle_indefinite Continuation markers for days and cycles respectively. They do not extend the returned rows. timing_status Whether timing was calculated, assumed or unresolved.

decay_days=0 returns dosing rows without a decay tail. The default adds two days of decreasing intensity after each dose. These extra rows represent a projection, not extra administrations, and intensity is not a dose amount. Overlapping rows keep the highest intensity.

Rows without a recognized route group or a resolved drug are excluded. A day choice with a resolved drug and route remains as a row with day NULL and an unresolved status. The frame can therefore cover only part of a variant's instructions.

administration_matrix() pivots the frame by drug and cycle-local day, taking the highest intensity across matching rows. It combines repeated cycles and omits days with no entries. Use the timeline below when individual cycles or dates matter.

docs.title: Calculate a treatment timeline
docs.text:
from datetime import date
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.analytics.treatment.scheduling import roll_out_variant

timeline = roll_out_variant(variant, start_date=date(2026, 1, 1), decay_days=0)
timeline[["sig_id", "phase", "cycle_number", "day", "elapsed_day", "calendar_date", "timing_status"]]

docs.title: Days and dates
docs.text:
Column Meaning day Day within the cycle, using the source notation. phase_elapsed_day Zero-based day relative to the phase's first explicit cycle. elapsed_day Zero-based day relative to variant start. calendar_date A timezone-free datetime.date, when start_date is supplied and timing can be calculated.

For example, two 21-day cycles with doses on days 1 and 8 produce:

Cycle day elapsed_day Date for a 1 January 2026 start 1 1 0 1 January 1 8 7 8 January 2 1 21 22 January 2 8 28 29 January

If an earlier phase has an unknown duration, variant-relative days and dates remain NULL. Phase-relative days can still be available for a later phase whose internal timing is known. An unresolved block also has a NULL phase-relative day.

With start_date, month and year cycles use calendar arithmetic. If a phase's start date is unknown, their phase-relative offsets are also NULL. Without start_date, calculations use 30-day months and 365-day years.

docs.title: Timing rules and status
docs.text:
Phases are ordered by phase_step. Cycle blocks within them are placed using their cycle numbers and cycle lengths:

Source timing Result Adjacent cycle ranges The following block starts after the preceding block. Overlapping cycle numbers Blocks share a cycle anchor. Different lengths overlapping across more than one shared cycle leave the later block unresolved. Several preceding blocks end together with different cycle lengths The following block is unresolved. A phase continues immediately after its predecessor's last cycle number Cycle numbering continues into that phase. A continuing-cycle marker has no finite end A later phase cannot be placed from that marker. timing_status Meaning resolved Timing could be calculated. resolved_via_fallback: ... Timing uses a stated assumption. Optional cycles are assumed given. unresolved: ... Required timing is missing or ambiguous; the message gives the reason.

Missing or tied phase steps leave all variant-relative dates NULL. A gap in phase steps leaves dates NULL from the later phase onward. From the first optional cycle, and in later phases, status records the assumption that optional cycles were given.

A choice-only instruction, such as one dose on a day between 7 and 15, remains in the result with day NULL and an unresolved: choice of days ... status. No alternative is selected automatically.

docs.title: Components and source fields
docs.text:
Timeline rows include sig_id, component, component_cui, phase, timing_sequence and the cycle-length bounds, unit and selection used for the calculation. Use these fields to trace a row back to its instruction. day_indefinite and cycle_indefinite retain separate day and cycle continuation markers.

modality is systemic, radiation, or NULL for an unclassified sig. Radiation rows can have no resolved drug. Pass systemic_only=True to omit radiation rows from the output; their phases still contribute to subsequent timing.

docs.title: Treatment analytics
docs.text: Treatment analytics are where HemOnc rows acquire reusable treatment meaning. The key discipline is to keep the policy explicit: HemOnc supplies source labels and relationships, while the selection spec or classification function states how your application interprets them.

docs.title: Classify a variant
docs.text:
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.analytics.treatment.classification import (
    is_concurrent_chemort,
    is_rt_only,
)

if is_concurrent_chemort(variant):
    print("radiation and systemic sigs are both confidently classified")
elif is_rt_only(variant):
    print("all sigs are confidently classified as radiation")

An unknown or NULL class_field is unknown. It does not count as systemic treatment and prevents a confident radiation-only or concurrent-chemoradiotherapy classification. Treating “unclassified” as “not present” would turn missing source information into a clinical conclusion.

docs.title: Classify drug ancestry
docs.text: Use is_endocrine_regimen() to identify variants whose drugs are all endocrine therapies, and is_supportive_regimen() to identify variants whose drugs are all growth-factor therapies. Here, “supportive” specifically means growth-factor ancestry. The same classifications are available for cycle blocks through is_endocrine_block() and is_supportive_block().

docs.title: Query and apply the ancestry index
docs.text:
Install the OMOP integration and configure the vocabulary connection's search path to expose its OMOP tables. Query an index from the source drug records and vocabulary relationships, then pass it to the classifiers or scheduling helpers:

from hemonc_alchemy.integrations.omop import main_class_ancestry
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.analytics.treatment.classification import (
    is_endocrine_regimen,
    is_supportive_regimen,
)
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.analytics.treatment.scheduling import cycle_block_templates

index = main_class_ancestry(source_session, omop_session=vocabulary_session)
endocrine = is_endocrine_regimen(variant, ancestry=index)
supportive = is_supportive_regimen(variant, ancestry=index)
blocks = cycle_block_templates(variant, ancestry=index)

Omit omop_session when the source session can also access the vocabulary tables. Classifiers can infer the session from attached source objects; supplying an index also supports detached objects and separate databases.

docs.title: Interpret the classification
docs.text:
The predicates and CycleTemplate.endocrine_regimen / supportive_regimen flags have three possible results:

Result Meaning True Every identified drug belongs to a fully resolved group with the requested ancestry. False A known group excludes the requested ancestry, or there are no drug entries to classify. None The available evidence cannot establish the classification, for example because a group is unresolved or the vocabulary is unavailable.

Drug ancestry uses active HemOnc Is a relationships beneath Endocrine therapeutic (44970) and Growth factor (20221). These are HemOnc concept codes. Classification applies to whole Drugs.main_class groups: every component in the group must have a usable Component Class edge. The polyhierarchical Steroid target (45523) is excluded. An incomplete group is unresolved; disagreement between fully resolved components is inconsistent.

A drug with NULL main_class, or a canonical drug instruction without a matching drug record, supplies unknown evidence. A known exclusion still yields False; otherwise unknown evidence yields None. Radiation and generic non-canonical component instructions without drug records are outside the drug ancestry scope.

docs.title: Investigate an unresolved result
docs.text:
Check index.unavailable_reason for a vocabulary availability problem. For individual groups, index.resolutions exposes the status, all component CUIs and the CUIs lacking usable classification edges:

resolution = index.resolutions.get(drug.main_class)
if resolution is not None:
    print(resolution.status.value)
    print(resolution.component_cuis)
    print(resolution.unresolved_cuis)

The index is cached per source/vocabulary engine pair. After reloading either dataset, call main_class_ancestry.cache_clear() or restart the process so subsequent queries use the refreshed data.

docs.title: Query standalone radiation
docs.text:
from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.analytics.treatment.filters import (
    find_standalone_radiation_sigs,
)

sigs = find_standalone_radiation_sigs(session, [condition_cui])

“Standalone” is a precise query policy: a radiation-classified sig with regimen Radiation therapy, no variant_cui, and a normalized study link to one of the requested condition CUIs. It does not prove that the entire study contains no systemic treatment.

docs.title: Select variants
docs.text:
Describe the selection as a plain spec, then execute it:

from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.analytics.treatment.selection import (
    ComponentRequirement,
    TreatmentSelectionSpec,
    select_variants,
)

spec = TreatmentSelectionSpec.for_conditions(
    [condition_cui],
    component_requirements=(ComponentRequirement.from_terms("cisplatin"),),
    version_policy="latest",
)
variants = select_variants(session, spec)

Component terms within one requirement are alternatives; separate requirements are combined. Category requirements work the same way, but require an application-supplied mapping from a source field to the category names used by the spec:

from hemonc_alchemy.toolkit.analytics.treatment.selection import CategoryRequirement

spec = TreatmentSelectionSpec.for_conditions(
    [condition_cui],
    category_requirements=(CategoryRequirement("cytotoxic", 1),),
)
variants = select_variants(
    session,
    spec,
    category_mapping={"main_class": {"Platinum agent": "cytotoxic"}},
)

The mapping is policy, not a hidden property of the model. Read source values before building a production mapping and decide how unmapped classes should be handled.

build_variant_query_artifacts() exposes the component projection, category projection, matching variant identities, and final statement. Use it when a selection needs auditability or returns an unexpected volume.
